question: Explain Image Representation in computers: Grayscale vs RGB vs HSV color spaces, channels, and pixel matrices.
idealAnswer: Digital images are multidimensional arrays of pixel intensity values. RGB stores Red, Green, and Blue additive channels. HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) separates color tone (Hue) from lighting intensity (Value), making it far more robust for color-based object segmentation under variable illumination.

explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Fundamentals and Color Spaces & Image Representations comprehension.

question: Explain Classical Image Processing Filters: Gaussian Blur (smoothing), Sobel Operator (edge detection), and Canny Edge Detector.
idealAnswer: Gaussian Blur convolves with a 2D Gaussian kernel to reduce high-frequency noise. Sobel computes horizontal and vertical image gradient derivatives. Canny edge detector combines Gaussian filtering, Sobel gradients, Non-Maximum Suppression (thinning edges), and Hysteresis Thresholding.
ideal_answer: Gaussian Blur convolves with a 2D Gaussian kernel to reduce high-frequency noise. Sobel computes horizontal and vertical image gradient derivatives. Canny edge detector combines Gaussian filtering, Sobel gradients, Non-Maximum Suppression (thinning edges), and Hysteresis Thresholding.
explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Classical CV and Image Filters & Canny Edge Detection comprehension.

question: What are Classical Feature Extractors: SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform), SURF, and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF)?
idealAnswer: SIFT detects scale-space extrema using Difference of Gaussians (DoG), providing robust scale- and rotation-invariant feature descriptors (patented/computationally heavy). ORB is a fast, open-source binary alternative combining FAST corner detection and BRIEF descriptors.
ideal_answer: SIFT detects scale-space extrema using Difference of Gaussians (DoG), providing robust scale- and rotation-invariant feature descriptors (patented/computationally heavy). ORB is a fast, open-source binary alternative combining FAST corner detection and BRIEF descriptors.
explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Feature Extraction and SIFT vs ORB Feature Matching comprehension.

question: Explain Object Detection Paradigms: Two-Stage Detectors (R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN with RPN) vs One-Stage Detectors (YOLO, SSD).
idealAnswer: Two-Stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) first generate candidate region proposals via a Region Proposal Network (RPN) and then classify/refine bounding boxes in a second stage (high accuracy, slower). One-Stage detectors (YOLO, SSD) treat detection as a single regression problem, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities in a single pass (real-time FPS).
ideal_answer: Two-Stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) first generate candidate region proposals via a Region Proposal Network (RPN) and then classify/refine bounding boxes in a second stage (high accuracy, slower). question: Explain Intersection over Union (IoU), Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS), and Mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95) in Object Detection.
idealAnswer: IoU measures overlap: Area of Overlap / Area of Union between predicted and ground-truth boxes. Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) removes redundant overlapping bounding boxes by iteratively discarding boxes with high IoU relative to the highest-confidence prediction. mAP calculates the mean area under the precision-recall curve across all classes.
ideal_answer: IoU measures overlap: Area of Overlap / Area of Union between predicted and ground-truth boxes. Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) removes redundant overlapping bounding boxes by iteratively discarding boxes with high IoU relative to the highest-confidence prediction. mAP calculates the mean area under the precision-recall curve across all classes.
explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Object Detection Metrics and IoU, NMS, and mAP Evaluation comprehension.

question: Explain Semantic Segmentation (U-Net, DeepLab with Atrous/Dilated Convolutions) vs Instance Segmentation (Mask R-CNN) vs Panoptic Segmentation.
concept: Semantic vs Instance vs Panoptic Segmentation
idealAnswer: Semantic Segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel without distinguishing individual instances (e.g. U-Net). Instance Segmentation detects and segments each individual distinct object instance (Mask R-CNN). Panoptic Segmentation unifies both, segmenting all countable instances and background stuff classes.
ideal_answer: Semantic Segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel without distinguishing individual instances (e.g. U-Net). explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Image Segmentation and Semantic vs Instance vs Panoptic Segmentation comprehension.

question: Explain Vision Transformers (ViT): Patch Extraction, Linear Projection, Class Token ([CLS]), and Self-Attention on image patches.
idealAnswer: ViT splits an image into non-overlapping patches (e.g. 16x16 pixels), flattens and linearly projects them into patch embeddings, prepends a learnable [CLS] token, adds 1D positional encodings, and processes them through standard Transformer encoder blocks without convolutions (trading inductive bias for global context at scale).

question: What is Optical Flow (Lucas-Kanade vs Farneback methods) in Video Processing for motion tracking across consecutive frames?
idealAnswer: Optical Flow calculates apparent pixel motion vectors between consecutive video frames based on the Brightness Constancy Assumption. Lucas-Kanade is a sparse differential method assuming uniform motion in local pixel neighborhoods. Farneback computes dense flow fields across all pixels.
ideal_answer: Optical Flow calculates apparent pixel motion vectors between consecutive video frames based on the Brightness Constancy Assumption. question: Explain Face Detection and Recognition Pipelines: Face Alignment, MTCNN / RetinaFace, and Face Embeddings (FaceNet with Triplet Loss).
idealAnswer: Pipeline: 1) Face Detection locates faces and facial landmarks (RetinaFace); 2) Alignment normalizes pose; 3) Deep network (FaceNet) maps facial crops to compact 128D/512D unit-sphere embeddings trained with Triplet Loss (minimizing anchor-positive distance and maximizing anchor-negative distance).

question: What is Anchor-Free Object Detection (CenterNet, FCOS) and how does it simplify detection compared to predefined anchor boxes?
idealAnswer: Traditional detectors require manual tuning of anchor box aspect ratios and scales. Anchor-free models (FCOS, CenterNet) treat objects as points (e.g. bounding box centers), directly predicting bounding box boundary distances (l, t, r, b) or Gaussian peak keypoints per pixel, eliminating anchor hyperparameter tuning.

question: Explain Data Augmentation techniques in Computer Vision: Mixup, CutMix, Mosaic, Albumentations, and Geometric Transformations.
idealAnswer: Augmentation artificially expands training diversity to prevent overfitting. Standard augmentations include random crops, flips, and color jitter. Advanced augmentations: Mixup blends two images and their labels linearly; CutMix replaces an image patch with a patch from another image; Mosaic stitches 4 images into one (YOLO).
ideal_answer: Augmentation artificially expands training diversity to prevent overfitting. Standard augmentations include random crops, flips, and color jitter. Advanced augmentations: Mixup blends two images and their labels linearly; CutMix replaces an image patch with a patch from another image; Mosaic stitches 4 images into one (YOLO).
explanation: Evaluates Computer Vision Data Augmentation and Modern CV Data Augmentation (Mixup/CutMix) comprehension.

question: What is Spatial Pyramid Pooling (SPP) and Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) for Multi-Scale Object Detection?
idealAnswer: FPN combines low-resolution, semantically strong deep feature maps with high-resolution, semantically weak shallow feature maps via a top-down pathway and lateral connections. This constructs rich multi-scale feature pyramids that detect small, medium, and large objects accurately.

question: Explain Image Similarity and Contrastive Learning in Computer Vision: SimCLR, MoCo, and InfoNCE Loss.
idealAnswer: Contrastive learning learns representations without human labels. SimCLR creates two augmented views of the same image (positive pair) and maximizes their cosine similarity while pushing apart representations of other images in the batch (negative pairs) using InfoNCE loss.
ideal_answer: Contrastive learning learns representations without human labels. SimCLR creates two augmented views of the same image (positive pair) and maximizes their cosine similarity while pushing apart representations of other images in the batch (negative pairs) using InfoNCE loss.

question: What are Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting for novel view 3D scene synthesis?
idealAnswer: NeRF uses an MLP to represent continuous 5D scenes (3D coordinates + 2D viewing direction) and synthesizes novel camera views via volume rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting replaces MLPs with millions of 3D ellipsoidal Gaussians rasterized via tile-based GPU sorting for real-time 100+ FPS rendering.

question: How do you deploy Computer Vision models at the Edge using TensorRT, OpenVINO, and ONNX Runtime for low-latency inference?
idealAnswer: Export PyTorch/TensorFlow models to ONNX. TensorRT (NVIDIA GPUs) and OpenVINO (Intel CPUs) optimize computation graphs by performing layer and tensor fusion, kernel autotuning, dynamic memory pooling, and FP16/INT8 precision quantization for real-time edge performance.
